case_title: Javed Masood and Anr. v. State of Rajasthan
accused_victim_relationship: Prior enmity/dispute between the accused and PW-5 (the victim's brother, the FIR lodger), as admitted by PW-5 and noted by the Court; no accused-victim relationship described
statutory_provisions: IPC s.302 (charged with ss.147, 323, 324; trial convictions also under ss.148 and 201)
weapon: Gupties, swords, knives and gandasas (as alleged by the prosecution)
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW-5, PW-13, PW-14, rejected by the Court), police and independent witness testimony, medical (post-mortem)
trial_court_outcome: Convicted of ss.148, 201 and 302 IPC; sentence amount not stated
high_court_outcome: Conviction under s.302 IPC upheld; convictions under ss.148 and 201 set aside
neutral_facts: On the afternoon of 25 May 1999, around 12.30 p.m., the victim was at a tyre shop. The prosecution case was that about ten to twelve armed persons, carrying gupties, swords, knives and gandasas, surrounded the victim and attacked him, inflicting multiple incised and penetrating wounds to the head, face, neck, chest, abdomen, back and arms. The assailants then fled. A police vehicle reached the spot within minutes and took the victim to hospital, where he was declared dead. The report lodged by the victim's brother was registered as an FIR and investigated. A charge-sheet was filed against two named persons, and investigation against others was kept pending. The shop owner testified that the victim came alone on a motorcycle to repay a debt and talked with him for about 15 minutes. He then went to the basement, and on returning found the victim gone. He later found the victim dead in a pool of blood in the street. Police removed the body within five to ten minutes. He said the victim's brother arrived about ten minutes after the removal, and that he had given no names because he had not seen the attack. Three police witnesses, including the constable and driver who lifted the body, stated that the victim's brother and two other alleged eyewitnesses were not present. The post-mortem report recorded excessive haemorrhage from injuries to the right lung and liver as the cause of death. Three named eyewitnesses testified that they saw the attack.
physical_harm: Death of the victim from multiple incised and penetrating wounds; death attributed to haemorrhage from injuries to the right lung and liver
motive: alleged: incident arose out of acute enmity (defence contention); the Court did not decide the motive for the attack
key_evidence_accepted: Evidence of PW-6 (shop owner) that PW-5, PW-13 and PW-14 were not at the scene; corroborating police evidence of PW-18, PW-29 and PW-30; the post-mortem report. The Court rejected the eyewitness evidence of PW-5, PW-13 and PW-14.
witness_credibility: PW-5 (victim's brother) was a highly interested and partisan witness whose evidence was disbelieved; PW-13 and PW-14 were discarded; PW-6 and police witnesses PW-18, PW-29 and PW-30 were independent and reliable
post_offence_conduct: Alleged by the prosecution that the assailants fled the scene; the Court made no finding on this
trial_duration: offence: 25 May 1999; trial judgment: not given; High Court: 4.3.2008; Supreme Court: 09 March 2010
legal_representation: Appellants: A. Sharan, A.K. Singh, Samir Ali Khan. State: R. Gopalakrishnan
investigation_status: FIR registered; charge-sheet filed against the appellants; investigation kept pending under s.173(8) Cr.P.C. against others; trial completed
procedural_irregularity: The public prosecutor did not seek leave to declare PW-6 hostile; the prosecution never declared PWs 6, 18, 29 and 30 hostile
appeal_history: Trial court: convicted under ss.148, 201, 302. High Court: s.302 conviction upheld; ss.148 and 201 set aside. Supreme Court: appeal allowed; convictions and sentences set aside
prosecution_argument: Supported the judgment under appeal (convictions under s.302 IPC)
defence_argument: Presence of the eyewitnesses was highly doubtful; reliance placed on PW-6, PW-29, PW-18 and PW-30; the incident arose from acute enmity
legal_principle_applied: Concurrent findings are not usually disturbed under Article 136 unless vital evidence was ignored or the conclusion rests on evidence that cannot be accepted; the defence may rely on evidence of witnesses not declared hostile
precedent_relied_upon: Mukhtiar Ahmed Ansari v. State (NCT of Delhi), (2005) 5 SCC 258, which relied on Raja Ram v. State of Rajasthan, (2005) 5 SCC 272
other_sentence_order: Appellants directed to be released forthwith
